To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) over 10% (n = 686) of leisure boats in Sweden contain antifouling layers with >400 μ g Sn/cm(2), (ii) the majority of these boats have several coatings on top of the antifouling layer, and (iii) the antifou ling paints contain high loads of copper, even on boats sailing only in freshwater.

1) over 10% leisure boats have >400 μgm(-2) of tin present in their hull coatings, 2) the tin is likely to be present in coatings close the hull, 3) high levels of copper are detected on boats sailing in fresh water, 4) many boat owners apply too many paint layers, and 5) the XRF method provides a fast and easy way to screen for high levels of tin and copper on leisure boats.

the use of TBT-containing antifouling (AF) coatings on leisure boats has not been completely banned and that high levels of copper are detected in AF coatings even on boats that are sailing in freshwater.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the environmental risks from antifouling maintenance work on leisure boats and the risk from copper release into the aquatic environment.

the need to improve the environmental management of antifouling activities in Sweden, including a ban of copper and zinc in paints for leisure boats, as well as a better enforcement of the current regulations.
the need for better environmental labelling and more stringent regulation of antifouling products.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
TBT is no longer used as antifouling agent in Swedish leisure boats, but OT compounds, and in some cases also copper, is still present.
there is no reason for the EU to extend the ban on the use of TBT in antifouing paints to leisure boats.
the use of OT compounds in leisure boats is still a threat to the marine environment.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
there is a large number of leisure boats still containing TBT in their antifoulings.
the XRF analysis of antifouling coating paints on leisure boats is a useful and cost-effective tool for monitoring compliance with legislation and for detecting potential environmental risks.

the XRF measurements show that the majority of the leisure boats in the studied area are still coated with antifouling containing TBT, and that the use of copper-based antifouling is still common practice.
The main takeaway from our work is that
XRF analysis is a useful tool for monitoring antifouling activities on leisure boats, which is a first step in the right direction to reduce the release of TBT and copper to the environment.
there is a need to improve the knowledge on how to safely remove OT coatings from leisure boats and to ensure that the new antifouling technologies do not pose an additional environmental risk.
the XRF technique can be used for screening of antifouling coating composition and thickness, which is useful information for the authorities and boat owners.
